definition.text: Proposed framing, because the evidence does not cleanly support it as a separate element: this reference model treats Compute Resources (CPU/GPU pools, autoscaling) as distinct from Runtime/Sandbox isolation (3.3) and Isolated Runtime Profiles (4.1), but the fetched evidence shows the same system typically does both jobs at once -- a per-tenant Firecracker microVM is simultaneously the isolation boundary and the unit of CPU/GPU allocation, and Kata Containers/gVisor appear in both this card's and 3.3's evidence under the same names. This repo's own three-way card split (3.3 / 4.1 / 4.2) is our design's own bucketing choice, not one the evidence forces.

landscape.text: The real tradeoff is isolation/simplicity versus density: dedicated per-tenant microVMs (Firecracker) give hardware isolation and scale-to-zero economics but leave capacity idle between tenants, while GPU-sharing mechanisms trade isolation for density -- time-slicing (software-only, zero memory isolation, up to 48 concurrent), MIG (hardware-partitioned, up to 7 slices per H100) and MPS (concurrent kernel execution, limited fault protection). The measured cost of not sharing is stark: "Average GPU utilization in production Kubernetes clusters is just 5%, according to the Cast AI 2026 State of Kubernetes Optimization Report." This repo's own compute resources are a fixed local/rented GPU fleet (F-a4-02) rather than a shared, autoscaled pool, so none of these sharing mechanisms currently apply here -- a hosted model API needs none of this at all, since "Serverless APIs abstract these hardware complexities, allowing you to avoid GPU shortages, quota limits, and provisioning delays."

evidence.quote: Average GPU utilization in production Kubernetes clusters is just 5%, according to the Cast AI 2026 State of Kubernetes Optimization Report.
Serverless APIs abstract these hardware complexities, allowing you to avoid GPU shortages, quota limits, and provisioning delays.

usage.text: The closest real illustration found of a compute-resource request shaped as a declaration rather than a raw device count is Kubernetes DRA: "app operators don't need to specify device quantities in Pod resource requests; instead, the Pod references a resource claim, and the device configuration in that claim applies to the Pod." This is not confirmed as this repo's own implementation -- this repo's actual usage is a fixed named GPU inventory (the `f-` prefixed contracts) rather than a claim-based API; per this repo's own target framing, callers reach compute only indirectly, in that "a fleet of GPUs serves local models" behind one model-gateway call, never a bare device request.

gaps.what: No standard applies: standards is an empty array because no standards-track spec was found governing fleet compute-resource allocation for agent sandboxes (CPU/GPU pooling, autoscaling policy). Kubernetes DRA is the closest schema found, but it is a project API, not a cross-runtime standard the way the OCI Runtime Spec is.
gaps.why_it_matters: Without a standard, a caller's compute-resource request is not portable across a Kubernetes-DRA fleet, a Run:ai-scheduled fleet, and a Modal-style container pool -- three different call shapes for the same underlying need.
gaps.research_query: is there an emerging cross-runtime standard for declaring a fractional or claim-based compute resource request

gaps.what: This repo's own compute-resource pool (six named local/rented GPU contracts) has no measured utilization figure to compare against the cited industry average of 5% (best cluster 49%).
gaps.why_it_matters: Without a measured number, it is unknown whether this repo's fixed-inventory model is efficient or leaves capacity idle the way unmanaged shared clusters do.
